messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Model
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Vignette:
Diane Martinez is a sixty-six-year-old model who has been widowed for nearly a decade, and she still works part-time for a small agency that books older women for commercial shoots. She came to therapy after her internist referred her following a physical exam that revealed elevated blood pressure and a persistent tremor in her hands—findings that Diane herself had chalked up to getting older. But the truth, as she finally admitted to herself in the waiting room, was that she had not felt calm or safe in the four years since the morning she accidentally killed a young woman with her car.

Diane had been driving to a location shoot in the suburbs, a familiar route she had taken dozens of times. It was raining lightly, and she was thinking about the lighting setup the photographer wanted. She did not see the cyclist until the impact, until the body—a twenty-three-year-old art student named Maya—was thrown across the hood and onto the wet asphalt. Diane stopped immediately, called 911, stayed with the woman until the ambulance arrived. Maya died in the hospital later that day from a traumatic brain injury. The police report cited poor visibility and no fault; the district attorney declined to press charges. But from that moment, Diane’s internal narrative hardened into a single, unbearable sentence: *Someone else would not have let this happen.* She had been a professional who prided herself on precision and composure—her career depended on it—and she could not reconcile that identity with the fact that she had been the one behind the wheel.

In the months that followed, Diane developed a constellation of symptoms that she initially mistook for grief or exhaustion. She could not stop replaying the moment of impact in her mind, but what troubled her even more was the feeling that she was permanently humiliated. She told her therapist that she would never be able to look at herself again without seeing a person who had failed in the most fundamental way. The inaction guilt was specific and corrosive: she was certain that if she had simply glanced one more time to the right, or braked half a second earlier, Maya would still be alive. She began to avoid driving entirely, which meant she could no longer travel to shoots outside her immediate neighborhood. Her agent accommodated her for a while, but eventually Diane stopped taking jobs that required her to go anywhere she had not been before. Her work shrank to a handful of catalogue shoots done at a studio two blocks from her apartment, and she began to turn down jobs that involved outdoor scenes or street photography, because the sight of a bicycle rack or a crosswalk made her stomach drop.

Her body remained on permanent alert. At home, alone in her quiet condo, she could not relax. She would sit on the sofa with her shoulders hunched and her jaw clenched, scanning the room for no reason she could name. She had difficulty concentrating during shoots—forgetting simple poses, missing the photographer’s instructions, needing multiple retakes. Her colleagues noticed and whispered. Diane told herself it was early menopause or the stress of widowhood, but she knew better. She had become a person who was always waiting for danger, even in a safe room.

What finally brought her to therapy was an incident at the grocery store. She was standing in the checkout line when a child’s voice behind her shouted, “Mommy, look!”—and Diane dropped her basket, her heart pounding, a flash of rain and bicycle metal filling her vision. She fled the store without paying for her cart. That evening, sitting in her darkened living room, she called her doctor and said she needed help. She is afraid that she will never be free of the memory, but more than that, she is afraid of her own judgment: that she does not deserve to be free. She comes to each session hoping someone will tell her she is wrong about herself, but she does not quite believe that anyone can.
